questions.question: What does `tr:nth-child(odd)` select?
options: Every tr element that has an odd number of children
Every tr element that is in an odd position among its siblings
Every tr element with an odd-numbered class name
questions.explanation: nth-child selects elements based on their position among sibling elements, not based on properties of the element itself.

questions.question: What is required for `::before` or `::after` to actually render anything?
options: Nothing extra — they render automatically once styled
A `content` property must be set, even if it's just an empty string, or nothing renders regardless of other styles
The parent element must have position: relative
questions.explanation: Without a content property, a pseudo-element has nothing to generate and produces no visible output, even with background/border styles applied.

questions.question: Why is `::after` generated content considered inappropriate for information a user actually needs?
options: It renders slower than real DOM content
Generated content is not reliably exposed to assistive technology and cannot be selected as real text
It only works in one browser
It cannot contain any text at all
questions.explanation: Pseudo-element content lives outside the accessibility tree in a way real content doesn't, making it unsuitable for anything beyond decorative or supplementary content.

questions.question: What makes `:has()` different from traditional CSS combinators like `>` or `+`?
options: It only works with id selectors
It lets you style an element based on what it contains — effectively a parent/ancestor selector, which CSS previously had no equivalent for
It can only be used inside @keyframes
questions.explanation: Every other combinator selects based on relationships looking 'downward' or 'forward'; :has() is the first native CSS way to select an element based on its descendants, something that previously required JavaScript.
